extracted.intended_audience: journalists, media scholars, students of public opinion, and policymakers interested in the functioning and limits of the press
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts evaluative principles about what makes something 'news' and the institutional, technical, and psychological constraints on reporting and public information. Applies to analyses of news selection, newsroom practice, and the relationship between institutions and public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectification/naming/measurement prerequisite
rubrics_metrics.description: The more points objectified, measured, named, there are at which news can occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News is more likely when events can be named, measured and recorded; abstract, unmeasured phenomena do not readily become news. (Opening claim: events must be given shape and names to be reported as news.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious place or stereotyped shape reveals news
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually it is the stereotyped shape assumed by an event at an obvious place that uncovers the run of the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters find news in recognizable, stereotyped forms (e.g., a building leaning is news before it collapses). If an event fits an obvious shape or location, it is easier to recognize and report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of machinery of record determines certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever there is a good machinery of record, the modern news service works with great precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sectors with dependable recording (stock tickers, election tabulation, births/deaths, customs) yield precise, timely news; the presence of institutional record-keeping increases news reliability and speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of objective records makes topics debatable or neglected
rubrics_metrics.description: All news about states of mind ... descriptions of personalities, motives, public opinion, policies, private income, wages ... involve data that are at best spasmodically recorded. Then the news on these subjects is bound to be debatable, when it is not wholly neglected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subjects without systematic measurement or with hidden data are often contested or underreported; disputes, investigations or public controversies may be required to make them newsworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overt acts or signals create news out of complex conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The events which are not scored are reported either as personal and conventional opinions, or they are not news. They do not take shape until somebody protests, or somebody investigates, or somebody publicly makes an issue of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex, diffuse conditions (e.g., poor labor conditions) only become news when signaled by overt acts (strikes, walkouts, police summons); news routines wait for visible signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: News prioritized by immediate relevance to readers' lives
rubrics_metrics.description: The easiest way is to let the news be uncovered by the overt act and to describe the event as the story of interference with the reader's life. That is where his attention is first aroused, and his interest most easily enlisted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and reporters emphasize aspects of events that affect readers directly (inconvenience, danger, service interruptions) because such angles quickly attract and retain audience interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource and cost constraints limit investigative reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: To make plausible that conditions are bad, you need a good reporter, many columns of print... It is impossible to suppose that any daily newspaper could normally regard the making of Pittsburgh Surveys ... as one of its tasks. News which requires so much trouble as that to obtain is beyond the resources of a daily press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In-depth investigations demand time, money, specialized talent and space; routine daily papers cannot routinely supply these, so complex issues are often undercovered unless external actors initiate investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press agents shape the selection and presentation of facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The publicity man... presents him a clear picture of a situation out of which he might otherwise make neither head nor tail. But the picture which the publicity man makes for the reporter is the one he wishes the public to see. He is responsible only to his employers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organized publicity intermediaries (press agents) filter and package facts for reporters, advancing employers' interests; this introduces systematic bias and explains why organized groups hire press agents to manage media attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypes and standardized routines are necessary editorial tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Without standardization, without stereotypes, without routine judgments ... the editor would soon die of excitement. The final page is of a definite size... and in each caption there must be a definite number of letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deadlines, space limits, and the need for fast decisions force editors to rely on templates, stereotypes and routine judgments; these economize time but constrain subtle or unconventional reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic necessity to interest readers quickly shapes coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: It comes from the economic necessity of interesting the reader quickly, and the economic risk involved in not interesting him at all, or of offending him by unexpected news insufficiently or clumsily described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors favor formats and facts that will immediately engage audiences; awkward, complex, or unfamiliar angles are downgraded because they risk losing readers or provoking adverse reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision of news proportional to precision of recording
rubrics_metrics.description: The news... is precise in proportion to the precision with which the event is recorded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where events are objectively recorded, reports can be precise; where recording is imprecise or absent, reports are necessarily vague, debatable, or prone to competing interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicate source reliability instead of overstating claims
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no defense ... for stating six times that Lenin is dead, when the only information the paper possesses is a report that he is dead from a source repeatedly shown to be unreliable. The news... is not 'Lenin Dead' but 'Helsingfors Says Lenin is Dead.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalistic responsibility requires qualifying claims by the reliability of their sources; overstating unverified information is indefensible and misleads the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chaotic or censored situations favor propagandistic stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: The hardest thing to report is chaos... This put the formulating of Russian news at its source in Helsingfors, Stockholm, Geneva, Paris and London ... propagandists. They were for a long time subject to no check ... they created ... stereotypes so evocative of hate and fear that the very best instinct of journalism ... was crushed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When direct access is blocked and events are chaotic, third-party censors/propagandists can dominate narratives and produce powerful but unreliable stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recorded legal/administrative facts allow exact tests; human affairs do not
rubrics_metrics.description: Once he departs from the region where it is definitely recorded at the County Clerk's office that John Smith has gone into bankruptcy, all fixed standards disappear... The story of why John Smith failed ... can be told in a hundred different ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sectors grounded in clear public records (legal filings, registry data) are subject to objective reporting standards; social, moral, and individual narratives lack such discipline and permit many interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial operational constraints require swift, composite judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Every bulletin requires a swift but complicated judgment. It must be understood, put in relation to other bulletins also understood, and played up or played down according to its probable interest for the public, as the editor conceives it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors must rapidly synthesize incoming items, weight their relative importance, and make publication choices under pressure of time, libel exposure, and commercial competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readers prefer news mapped onto their familiar experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless independent tests of checking the facts exist, the newspaper, if it is to be interesting, must make the reader perceive events as a new version of his familiar experience and translate them into acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News that connects to the reader's own experiences or immediate concerns will be more compelling; distant or abstract issues require translation into familiar terms to gain attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: News routines systematically disadvantage unorganized or less-institutionalized groups
rubrics_metrics.description: As long as real law and order do not exist, the bulk of the news will, unless consciously and courageously corrected, work against those who have no lawful and orderly method of asserting themselves... the bulletins from the scene of action will note the trouble that arose from the assertion, rather than the reasons which led to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Groups lacking institutional forms, records, or orderly channels (e.g., workers) are often reported only when disruptive acts occur; the deeper causes of grievances are marginalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press is not a substitute for institutional intelligence and record-keeping
rubrics_metrics.description: The press is no substitute for institutions... The remedy lies in social organization based on statistical analysis and record... the more intelligent and formally reported a community is, the more adequate will be the press as servant and guardian of institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate public information depends on institutions that collect, analyze and present data (bureaus, audits, statistics); strengthening such organized intelligence is the long-term remedy for press shortcomings.
